items.title: How New Zealand’s biggest city solved its housing crisis
items.blurb: Rezoning reshaped New Zealand's largest city — the clearest test yet of whether upzoning fixes housing, though the FT notes critics doubt the lesson transfers.

items.title: Economists should be worried about birth rates
items.author: Noah Smith
items.blurb: Smith pushes back on economists who wave away falling fertility, arguing that an aging and shrinking population is a threat worth taking seriously.

items.title: AI tool lets researchers 'vibe code' in the quantum realm
items.author: Davide Castelvecchi
items.blurb: An autonomous agent now writes and executes quantum-computing code on its own, though Castelvecchi reports it still needs a human hand at points.

items.title: Exclusive: NSF set to issue lowest number of new grants in four decades
items.author: Dan Garisto
items.blurb: The US science-funding agency is withholding $1 billion of its budget so the money can go to a special White House project, leaving it on track for its fewest new grants in four decades.

items.title: A China Strategy That Lasts
items.author: Bill Cassidy
items.blurb: Cassidy argues that a China policy durable enough to outlast a single administration has to be written by Congress rather than improvised by the executive.

items.title: What if our biggest problems aren’t economic?
items.author: Noah Smith
items.blurb: Noah Smith makes the case that the defining challenge of the new century is social rather than economic.

items.title: Childhood Exposure to Joint Custody Reforms and Adult Family Formation
items.author: Tyler Cowen
items.blurb: Across 13 million observations and staggered US state adoption, childhood exposure to joint-custody reform cuts adult fertility by 7 percent, symmetrically for women and men.

items.title: Frontier-technology markets are too narrow — here’s how to widen them
items.author: Luisa Corrado, Paul Kattuman
items.blurb: Governments must keep procurement processes as open as possible or face technological lock-in later, two economists argue.

items.author: Xuegong Zhang
items.blurb: With submissions rising and manuscripts growing more complex, a Tsinghua University researcher argues journals should give reviewers sanctioned AI tools rather than blanket bans that are hard to monitor and protect confidentiality only imperfectly.

items.title: More than 18,000 questionable images found in antibody catalogues of 15 companies
items.author: Dan Garisto
items.blurb: A science sleuth's audit of commercial antibody catalogues turned up more than 18,000 suspect images, raising questions for researchers working to improve the reliability of the reagents underpinning much of biomedicine.

items.title: AI-detection tools have made huge leaps forward — how good are they?
items.author: Miryam Naddaf
items.blurb: Scientists and publishers are testing a new breed of software that promises impressive accuracy at spotting AI-written text.

items.title: The Western water crisis has a simple solution
items.author: Matthew Yglesias
items.blurb: Yglesias frames the American West's water shortage as a pricing failure: the majority of the water is given away to farmers for almost nothing.

items.title: Does Donald Trump deserve credit for a manufacturing revival?
items.blurb: An assessment of whether the president's promise to bring back factory jobs is showing up in the employment numbers.

items.title: Do Minimum Wages Help Workers in Poor and Low-Income Families?
items.author: Tyler Cowen
items.blurb: Using survey data that oversamples poor households, a new paper reports adverse rather than beneficial effects of minimum wages on the employment and hours of the low-income workers they target.

items.title: China is changing the shape of global health. The terms are still up for negotiation
items.author: Ruby Wang
items.blurb: Chinese health-care partnerships supply other nations with cheap diagnostics and medicines; the open question is whether global institutions can ensure the deals also build local capacity and preserve sovereignty.

items.title: Mark Carney must beware an all-out trade war
